newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OLYMPICS-CAPE TOWN MAKE THE PACE IN THE SLOGAN RACE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-CAPE TOWN MAKE THE PACE IN THE SLOGAN RACE.

text.p: If slogans are significant in the race to stage the 2004 Olympics, Cape Town should romp home unchallenged.

So far the bid company has come up with "South Africa -- many cultures, one nation", "Southern Africa -- one region, one destiny", "Africa -- many nations, one continent" and "Five continents, one world".
The company remains relentlessly upbeat about bringing the Games to Africa for the first time.
Cape Town is trading heavily on the Nelson Mandela factor, hoping the International Olympic Committee will overlook problems such as crime, gale-force winds and rudimentary transport facilities.
The bid book presented by the city opens on a high moral tone with a quote from President Mandela's inauguration speech in May 1994:

"We enter with a covenant that we shall build a society in which all South Africans will be able to walk tall...assured of their inalienable right to human dignity -- a rainbow nation at peace with itself and the world."
Awarding the Games elsewhere, the book implies, would be a slap in the face for the saintly statesman who slew the apartheid dragon.
In case anyone misses the point about Mandela, the company in charge of organising the bid has also roped in Archbishop Desmond Tutu, one of South Africa's other Nobel peace prize winners.
"There is no other prospective miracle that will stem South Africa's slide into poverty and despair," Tutu said in a promotion for the bid company.
The archbishop said the Games -- which have yet to be held in Africa -- would help to bridge the gap between rich whites and poverty-stricken blacks which he said was the legacy of apartheid.
But not all South Africans are convinced they want the Games to take place in the shadow of spectacular Table Mountain.
Environmentalists complain that construction and visitors will crush wide swathes of Cape Town's proteas, the national flower, and other vegetation.

Activists campaigning for affordable housing for the tens of thousands of blacks living in sprawling slums around Cape Town say the accommodation planned for athletes, media and spectators would be too expensive to be used by the poor after the foreigners have gone home.
"The miracle that has characterised the recent political transformation of South Africa would be sustained beyond 2004," the company said.

"A 2004 Games in Cape Town would give new expression to the Olympic Movement... by demonstrating its power as an important social force through its capacity to make a significant difference to the lives of underprivileged people."
The bid company has proposed the government bring forward planned rail and road projects to the value of 900 million rand ($200 million) to provide adequate transport by 2004.
It estimates the Games will lead to an increase of about 250,000 people a day in Cape Town, and plans to house at least some of them in luxury liners moored in the harbour.

The company foresees total capital expenditure on the Games of 7.25 billion rand, with the central government picking up about half the bill, and predicts that up to 90,000 new jobs could be created in southern Africa if Cape Town wins the bid.
On crime and security, the bid company notes that Cape Town has successfully hosted visits by heads of state and many of the matches of the 1995 Rugby World Cup.
